topics.title: Piggy-bank ratios lie on a line through the origin

real_life_application.question: Cricket squad has batsmen and bowlers in ratio 3:1. Total squad = 20. How many batsmen?
real_life_application.explanation: Ratio 3:1 of 20 gives 15 batsmen and 5 bowlers, since 3/4 of 20 is 15.

real_life_application.question: Bakery sells items A and B in ratio 2:1. Of 30 orders, how many A orders?
real_life_application.explanation: Ratio 2:1 of 30 gives 20 A items and 10 B items, since 2/3 of 30 is 20.

real_life_application.question: Classroom has boys and girls in ratio 2:1. Total students = 30. How many girls?
real_life_application.explanation: Ratio 2:1 of 30 means 20 boys and 10 girls, since 1/3 of 30 is 10.

real_life_application.question: Factory produces two bulb types in ratio 5:1. Daily production = 600. Type-1 count?
real_life_application.explanation: Ratio 5:1 of 600 gives 500 type-1 bulbs and 100 type-2, since 5/6 of 600 is 500.

real_life_application.question: Town adults and children are in ratio 4:1. Town = 5000. How many adults?
real_life_application.explanation: Ratio 4:1 of 5000 gives 4000 adults and 1000 children, since 4/5 of 5000 is 4000.

topics.title: Houses lie on a horizontal line

real_life_application.question: Grid-city delivery stops at (0,1), (2,1), (4,1). What y-value do they share?
real_life_application.explanation: All three points have second coordinate 1, so they share y = 1.

real_life_application.question: Slope of horizontal line y = 1 is:
real_life_application.explanation: A horizontal line has rise 0 for any run, so its slope is zero.

real_life_application.question: Points (2,1), (3,1), (4,1). Are these three collinear?
real_life_application.explanation: All three points share y = 1, so they lie on one horizontal line and are collinear.

real_life_application.question: Three stops share y = 1. The y-intercept of the line is:
real_life_application.explanation: The line y = 1 crosses the y-axis where y = 1 and x = 0, so the y-intercept is 1.

real_life_application.question: Stops at (1,2), (2,2), (3,2). Equation of the line?
real_life_application.explanation: All three points share the same second coordinate 2, so the line is y = 2.

real_life_application.question: Car covers 60 km in 1 hour. Distance-time slope (km/h)?
real_life_application.explanation: Slope equals rise/run = 60 km / 1 h = 60, so the slope is sixty km/h.

real_life_application.question: Sales double every month: month 1 = 50, month 2 = 100. Slope of sales vs month?
real_life_application.explanation: From month 1 to 2 sales rose 100 − 50 = 50, so the slope of sales vs month is 50.

real_life_application.question: Taxi charges ₹10 per km. Fare vs distance slope (₹ per km)?
real_life_application.explanation: Each extra km adds ₹10 to the fare, so the slope of fare vs km is ten rupees.

real_life_application.question: Tap drips at 2 ml/min. Volume vs time slope (ml/min)?
real_life_application.explanation: Each minute the tap adds 2 ml, so the slope of volume vs time is two ml/min.

real_life_application.question: Sales double monthly: month 1 = 50, month 2 = 100. Is the line y = 50x?
real_life_application.explanation: Slope 50 passes through (1, 50) and (2, 100), matching the data, so the line is y = 50x.

topics.title: Why y = mx passes through origin

real_life_application.question: Car fuel starts at 50 L and stays at 50 L. Does fuel-time pass through origin?
real_life_application.explanation: At t = 0 fuel is already 50 L, so the graph starts at (0, 50), not at the origin.

real_life_application.question: Population model P = 0·t + 100. Does P-t pass through origin?
real_life_application.explanation: At t = 0 population equals 100, so the graph starts at (0, 100) and never goes through origin.

real_life_application.question: Spring obeys F = kx. Does F-x pass through origin?
real_life_application.explanation: At natural length x = 0 the spring exerts no force, so F = 0 and the line passes through origin.

real_life_application.question: Ohm's law V = IR. Does V-I graph pass through origin?
real_life_application.explanation: When current I = 0 voltage V = 0, so the V-I graph starts at the origin.

real_life_application.question: Subscription T = ax + b. T-x passes through origin when b equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Setting x = 0 gives T = b; this equals 0 only when b = 0, so b = 0 is required.

topics.title: y = 2x + 1 shifts the line off the origin

real_life_application.question: Phone plan costs ₹300/month + ₹0.50/min. What is the y-intercept (cost at 0 minutes)?
real_life_application.explanation: When minutes = 0 the monthly fixed fee ₹300 is the only charge, so the y-intercept is ₹300.

real_life_application.question: School admission: ₹1000 one-time + ₹500/month. At month 0 the fee is:
real_life_application.explanation: At month 0 only the one-time ₹1000 fee applies, so the y-intercept is ₹1000.

real_life_application.question: Printer charges ₹50 setup + ₹2/page. Slope of cost vs pages is:
real_life_application.explanation: Each extra page adds ₹2 to cost, so the slope is two rupees per page.

real_life_application.question: Water tank starts at 100 L and fills at 20 L/min. At t = 0 the volume is:
real_life_application.explanation: At t = 0 the tank already holds its initial 100 L, so the y-intercept is 100 litres.

real_life_application.question: Subscription ₹x/month + ₹y setup, T = ax + b. The intercept b represents:
real_life_application.explanation: Setting x = 0 leaves only the setup fee y, so the y-intercept b equals y rupees.

topics.title: Roles of slope a and intercept b

real_life_application.question: Spring obeys F = kx. In y = ax + b form, what is b?
real_life_application.explanation: F = kx + 0, so the intercept b is zero, meaning no offset force at natural length.

real_life_application.question: Depreciation V = 50000 − 800·t. The depreciation rate (slope a) per year is:
real_life_application.explanation: Each year the value falls by 800 rupees, so the slope a equals eight hundred rupees per year.

real_life_application.question: Revenue = price × quantity, with price fixed. Slope of revenue vs quantity is:
real_life_application.explanation: Each extra unit sold adds the fixed price to revenue, so the slope equals the price.

real_life_application.question: Celsius-Fahrenheit: F = (9/5)C + 32. Slope of F vs C is:
real_life_application.explanation: Each one-degree Celsius rise equals 9/5 degree Fahrenheit rise, so the slope is nine fifths.

real_life_application.question: Subscription ₹x/month with ₹y setup, T = ax + b. Slope a equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Each extra month adds the monthly fee, so the slope a equals the per-month charge.

real_life_application.question: Phones/covers: 2p + 3c = 70, 3p + 4c = 100. Matrix form is:
real_life_application.explanation: Combining the coefficients into A and the unknowns into x gives the form A·x = b.

real_life_application.question: For A = [[2,3],[3,4]] in the system above, the determinant is:
real_life_application.explanation: Det = 2·4 − 3·3 = 8 − 9 = −1, so the determinant of A is minus one.

real_life_application.question: Same system: 2x + 3y = 7, 3x + 4y = 10. Number of solutions is:
real_life_application.explanation: Determinant −1 ≠ 0 means the 2×2 matrix is invertible, so the system has exactly one solution.

real_life_application.question: Solve 2x + 3y = 7, 3x + 4y = 10. Phone price (x) is:
real_life_application.explanation: Solving gives x = 2 and y = 1, so the phone price is two dollars.

real_life_application.question: Same system. Cover price (y) is:
real_life_application.explanation: Solving gives x = 2 and y = 1, so the cover price is one dollar.

real_life_application.question: f(x) = 3x + 2. Solve f(α) = 17. α is:
real_life_application.explanation: 3α + 2 = 17 gives 3α = 15 so α = 5; the input value is number 5.

real_life_application.question: f(x) = 3x + 2. Solve f(α) = 17. f⁻¹(17) is:
real_life_application.explanation: The inverse value f⁻¹(17) is the same α = 5, expressed as five units.

real_life_application.question: f(x) = 3x + 2. f(0) equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Substituting x = 0 gives f(0) = 3·0 + 2 = 2, so the value is two units.

real_life_application.question: f(x) = 3x + 2. f(2) equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Substituting x = 2 gives f(2) = 3·2 + 2 = 8, so the value is number 8.

real_life_application.question: Is f(x) = 3x + 2 invertible over ℝ?
real_life_application.explanation: Slope 3 ≠ 0 means the line is non-horizontal and crosses every y = k exactly once, so f is invertible.

real_life_application.question: f(x) = x² − 10. f(5) equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Plugging x = 5 gives 5² − 10 = 25 − 10 = 15, so f(5) is number 15.

real_life_application.question: f(x) = x² − 10. f(0) equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Plugging x = 0 gives 0² − 10 = −10, so f(0) is number −10.

real_life_application.question: f(x) = x² − 10. f(10) equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Plugging x = 10 gives 10² − 10 = 100 − 10 = 90, so f(10) is number 90.

real_life_application.question: f(x) = x² − 10. f(−5) equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Plugging x = −5 gives (−5)² − 10 = 25 − 10 = 15, so f(−5) is also number 15.

real_life_application.question: Square plot side 5 m, cost = x² − 10 (thousands of ₹). Cost is:
real_life_application.explanation: x² − 10 = 25 − 10 = 15, so the cost is 15 thousand rupees = ₹15000.

real_life_application.question: α² − 10 = 54. Then α² equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Adding 10 to both sides gives α² = 54 + 10 = 64, so α² is number 64.

real_life_application.question: α² = 64. The two real solutions are:
real_life_application.explanation: The square root of 64 is 8, so the equation has solutions α = +8 and α = −8.

real_life_application.question: Distance² − 10 = kinetic energy. If KE = 54, the distance is:
real_life_application.explanation: Setting distance² = 64 gives distance = √64 = 8 (taking the positive root).

real_life_application.question: Ball height h = −t² + 100. If h = 99, then t is:
real_life_application.explanation: −t² + 100 = 99 ⇒ t² = 1 ⇒ t = 1, so the time is t = 1.

real_life_application.question: α² = 64 has how many real solutions?
real_life_application.explanation: Every positive k gives α² = k the two solutions α = ±√k, so exactly two real solutions exist.

real_life_application.question: g(x) = x³ − x² − 10x + 2. g(0) equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Plugging x = 0 gives 0 − 0 − 0 + 2 = 2, so g(0) is number 2.

real_life_application.question: g(x) = x³ − x² − 10x + 2. g(3) equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Plugging x = 3 gives 27 − 9 − 30 + 2 = −10, so g(3) is number −10.

real_life_application.question: g(x) = x³ − x² − 10x + 2. g(1) equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Plugging x = 1 gives 1 − 1 − 10 + 2 = −8, so g(1) is number −8.

real_life_application.question: g(x) = x³ − x² − 10x + 2. g(2) equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Plugging x = 2 gives 8 − 4 − 20 + 2 = −14, so g(2) is number −14.

real_life_application.question: g(-3) = -4 and g(-4) = -38. Between x = -4 and x = -3, g(x) = -22 has:
real_life_application.explanation: g(-4) = -38 < -22 < -4 = g(-3), so by IVT there is exactly one root in (-4, -3).

real_life_application.question: Earth surface point (latitude, longitude) is a vector in:
real_life_application.explanation: Two coordinates form an ordered pair, which lives in ℝ².

real_life_application.question: RGB color (r, g, b) with values in [0, 255] belongs to:
real_life_application.explanation: Three components form an ordered triple, so RGB colors live in ℝ³.

real_life_application.question: GPS location (x, y, z) is a point in:
real_life_application.explanation: Three coordinates x, y, z make an ordered triple, which lives in ℝ³.

real_life_application.question: Stock daily data (open, high, low, close) is a point in:
real_life_application.explanation: Four numbers give an ordered 4-tuple, so daily stock data lives in ℝ⁴.

real_life_application.question: A house with 5 features (size, rooms, age, ...) is a point in:
real_life_application.explanation: Five features form an ordered 5-tuple, so the house lies in ℝ⁵.

real_life_application.question: φ(x, y) = (2x+3y, 3x+4y). φ(1, 0) equals:
φ(x, y) = (2x+3y, 3x+4y). φ(0, 1) equals:
φ(x, y) = (2x+3y, 3x+4y). φ(1, 1) equals:
φ(x, y) = (2x+3y, 3x+4y). φ(0, 0) equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Plugging (0, 0) gives (0, 0); every linear map sends the origin to itself.

real_life_application.question: φ(x, y) = (2x+3y, 3x+4y) corresponds to which 2×2 matrix?
real_life_application.explanation: Columns are φ(1,0) = (2,3) and φ(0,1) = (3,4), giving the matrix [[2,3],[3,4]].

real_life_application.question: A = [[2,3],[3,4]]. The determinant is:
real_life_application.explanation: Det = 2·4 − 3·3 = 8 − 9 = −1, so the determinant of A is minus one.

real_life_application.question: A = [[1,2],[2,4]]. The determinant is:
real_life_application.explanation: Det = 1·4 − 2·2 = 4 − 4 = 0, so the determinant equals zero value.

real_life_application.question: Non-zero determinant means the system A·x = b has:
real_life_application.explanation: Det ≠ 0 means A is invertible, so A·x = b has exactly one solution x = A⁻¹·b.

real_life_application.question: Zero determinant (A = [[1,2],[2,4]]) means A is:
real_life_application.explanation: Det = 0 means A has no inverse, so A is not invertible.

real_life_application.question: Cramer's rule applies when the determinant is:
real_life_application.explanation: Cramer's rule divides by the determinant, so it works precisely when det ≠ 0 (non-zero).

topics.title: Matrix as a function ℝ² → ℝ²

real_life_application.question: Scaling matrix S(x, y) = (2x, 3y). Its matrix form is:
real_life_application.explanation: The diagonal entries scale x and y, so the matrix is [[2,0],[0,3]].

real_life_application.question: Reflection across the x-axis: (x, y) ↦ (x, −y). Its matrix is:
real_life_application.explanation: x stays the same and y flips sign, giving the diagonal matrix [[1,0],[0,-1]].

real_life_application.question: Shear matrix: (x, y) ↦ (x + y, y). Its matrix is:
real_life_application.explanation: First row (1, 1) gives x + y and second row (0, 1) gives y, so the matrix is [[1,1],[0,1]].

real_life_application.question: Projection onto the x-axis: (x, y) ↦ (x, 0). Its matrix is:
real_life_application.explanation: First row (1, 0) gives x and second row (0, 0) gives 0, so the matrix is [[1,0],[0,0]].

real_life_application.question: Image transform T(x, y) = (2x+3y, 3x+4y). T(1, 0) equals:
real_life_application.explanation: Plugging (1, 0) gives (2·1 + 3·0, 3·1 + 4·0) = (2, 3), the first column of the matrix.

real_life_application.question: A = [[1,2],[2,4]]. The condition A·(x, y) = (0, 0) is:
real_life_application.explanation: The first row gives x + 2y = 0; the second row is just twice this equation.

real_life_application.question: Solve x + 2y = 0 for x:
real_life_application.explanation: Subtracting 2y from both sides gives x = −2y, so x equals minus 2y.

real_life_application.question: All solutions of A·(x, y) = 0 are parametrised by:
real_life_application.explanation: Setting y = t and x = −2t gives the parametrisation (x, y) = (−2t, t) = (−2, 1)·t.

real_life_application.question: A = [[1,2],[2,4]] has rank:
real_life_application.explanation: Row 2 equals 2·Row 1, so only one row is independent; the rank is one.

real_life_application.question: Image of A = [[1,2],[2,4]] is the line:
real_life_application.explanation: Column 2 equals 2·Column 1, so the image is the line through (1, 2), which is y = 2x.
